introduction-what-is-a-binary.core: A binary is a file the kernel can turn into a running process. On Linux that's an ELF file: a header saying what CPU and type it is, program headers telling the loader which pieces to map into memory, and sections holding code, data, symbols and relocation info. Understanding the format explains startup errors, library problems, binary size and how tools like gdb or ldd work.

first_principles.problem: A binary built on a laptop fails on a server with 'cannot execute binary file: Exec format error'.
truths: The kernel needs a known format.
Code and data live in separate regions.

analogy.title: A flat-pack furniture kit
analogy.story: The box label says what it is and for which room; the instructions say which parts go where; the parts are the code and data.
analogy.breaks: Furniture is assembled once; binaries are mapped into memory on every run.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Exec format error explained: wrong architecture.

code.text:
file ./app
# app: ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, ARM aarch64, dynamically linked, interpreter /lib/ld-linux-aarch64.so.1
readelf -h ./app | grep -E 'Class|Machine|Type|Entry'
# Machine: AArch64  → won't run on x86_64 server

check.q: What does 'Exec format error' usually mean?
check.a: The binary's format or architecture (e.g. ARM vs x86_64) doesn't match what the kernel can execute.

anatomy-of-elf-sections-text-data-bss-ro.core: Sections group content by purpose. .text holds machine code (read and execute), .rodata constants and string literals (read-only), .data initialised globals (read-write), and .bss zero-initialised globals, which take no file space and are just a size the loader zero-fills. Others include .symtab and .dynsym for symbols, .rela for relocations, .plt and .got for dynamic calls, and .debug_* for debuggers. The loader maps them as segments with matching permissions.

first_principles.problem: A binary is 300 MB, and the team doesn't know whether it's code, data or debug info.

analogy.title: Rooms in a house with different locks
analogy.story: The workshop (code) is usable but not changeable, the library (constants) is read-only, and the storage room (data) is free to rearrange.
analogy.breaks: Houses don't zero rooms on entry; the loader zero-fills .bss.

code.text:
size ./app
#    text    data     bss     dec
# 8123456   23456  100352  ...
readelf -S --wide ./app | grep -E 'debug|text'
strip --strip-debug -o app.stripped ./app && ls -lh app app.stripped   # 300M → 9M

check.q: Why does .bss take no space in the file?
check.a: It holds zero-initialised data, so only its size is recorded and the loader allocates zeroed memory at runtime.

object-files-and-the-linking-process.core: Compiling turns each source file into a relocatable object file (.o) with code, data, a symbol table (defined and undefined symbols), and relocations: placeholders for addresses not yet known. The linker combines objects and libraries, resolves undefined symbols to definitions, lays out sections and patches the relocations into an executable or shared library. 'Undefined reference' and 'multiple definition' errors come from this step.

first_principles.problem: A build fails with 'undefined reference to curl_easy_init' even though the code compiles.
truths: Libraries must be named to the linker.

analogy.title: Writing chapters with 'see page ?' references
analogy.story: Each author writes a chapter with placeholders; the editor assembles the book and fills in page numbers.
analogy.breaks: Editors can guess missing chapters; linkers just fail.

code.text:
gcc -c main.c -o main.o
nm main.o | grep curl
#                 U curl_easy_init     (U = undefined)
gcc main.o -o app            # undefined reference
gcc main.o -o app -lcurl     # resolved

check.q: What does a 'U' next to a symbol in nm output mean?
check.a: The symbol is undefined in that object and must be resolved from another object or library at link time.

static-vs-dynamic-linking.core: Static linking copies library code into the executable, so it's self-contained, portable across distros and fast to start, but larger, and security fixes require rebuilding. Dynamic linking records dependencies (DT_NEEDED) and loads shared libraries (.so) at runtime: smaller binaries, shared memory pages and system-wide patching, at the cost of dependency hell (missing or incompatible versions). Containers and Go often favour static; distros favour dynamic.

first_principles.problem: A binary runs on Ubuntu but fails on Alpine with 'not found' because it needs glibc.
truths: Sharing code saves memory and patching effort.

analogy.title: Packing your own tools vs using the workshop's
analogy.story: Bring all your tools and you can work anywhere; rely on the workshop's tools and you travel light, but need the right workshop.
analogy.breaks: Tools don't get security patches; libraries do, and static binaries miss them.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Static binary runs anywhere with matching arch.

code.text:
ldd ./app-dyn
#   libssl.so.3 => /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libssl.so.3
#   libc.so.6 => /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o app-static .
file app-static   # statically linked → runs in FROM scratch

check.q: Why does a glibc-linked binary often fail on Alpine Linux?
check.a: Alpine uses musl libc, so the glibc shared libraries and loader the binary expects aren't present.

the-loader-ldso.core: For dynamically linked programs, the kernel maps the executable and then runs the interpreter named in PT_INTERP, the dynamic loader ld-linux.so. It reads DT_NEEDED entries, searches for libraries (RPATH/RUNPATH, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, ld.so.cache, default paths), maps them, performs relocations, runs initialisers, and jumps to main. Function calls resolve lazily via PLT and GOT unless BIND_NOW is set.

first_principles.problem: An app fails with 'error while loading shared libraries: libfoo.so.2: cannot open shared object file'.
truths: The kernel delegates linking to user space.
Search order determines which library loads.

analogy.title: A stage manager before the show
analogy.story: They gather every actor (library) the script lists, place them on stage, and cue the start.
analogy.breaks: Stage managers improvise for missing actors; the loader aborts.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: See exactly where the loader looked.

code.text:
LD_DEBUG=libs ./app 2>&1 | grep -E 'find library|trying file' | head
ldconfig -p | grep libfoo
readelf -d ./app | grep -E 'NEEDED|RUNPATH'
# fix: install lib, add RUNPATH, or ldconfig

check.q: Which environment variable shows the dynamic loader's library search in detail?

ld_preload-the-ultimate-hook.core: LD_PRELOAD tells the dynamic loader to load named shared libraries before all others, so their symbols win symbol resolution. That lets you override functions like malloc, open or connect without recompiling: for memory allocators (jemalloc), debugging, profiling, faking time, or sandboxing. It's also an attack vector (rootkits via /etc/ld.so.preload), and it's ignored for setuid binaries and has no effect on statically linked programs.

first_principles.problem: A team wants to try jemalloc for a closed-source binary without rebuilding it.
truths: The first definition wins symbol lookup.
Security restrictions apply to privileged binaries.
derivation: Write/obtain a **shared lib** defining the function.

analogy.title: A stand-in actor who goes on first
analogy.story: Whoever is on stage first gets the role, so slipping in a stand-in changes the performance without rewriting the play.
analogy.breaks: Stand-ins are visible; preloaded hooks are invisible to the app.

check.q: Why doesn't LD_PRELOAD affect statically linked binaries?
check.a: They don't use the dynamic loader; all code is already linked in, so there's no runtime symbol resolution to interpose.

vdso-the-virtual-library.core: Some syscalls, like clock_gettime and gettimeofday, are called extremely often, and a real syscall's mode switch is costly. The vDSO is a small shared library the kernel maps into every process (shown as [vdso] in /proc/self/maps) that implements them in user space by reading kernel-maintained data pages. Time reads cost nanoseconds without entering the kernel; libc calls it automatically.

first_principles.problem: A high-frequency trading app calls clock_gettime millions of times per second, and engineers worry about syscall overhead.
truths: Some data can be safely exposed read-only.
derivation: Falls back to **real syscall** if needed.
Clock source matters (**TSC** good, HPET slow).

analogy.title: A clock on the office wall vs calling the reception desk
analogy.story: Instead of phoning reception for the time, you glance at a clock they keep synchronised.
analogy.breaks: Wall clocks can be wrong; vDSO falls back if the clock source isn't usable.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Time calls avoid the kernel entirely.

code.text:
grep -E 'vdso|vvar' /proc/self/maps
cat /sys/devices/system/clocksource/clocksource0/current_clocksource   # tsc
strace -c -e clock_gettime ./bench   # ~0 syscalls: served by vDSO

check.q: Why might clock_gettime suddenly become slow on a VM?
check.a: If the clock source isn't vDSO-capable (e.g. HPET or certain hypervisor clocks), calls fall back to real syscalls.
